messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 78, Richard had spent decades building a life around order, logic, and predictability. He was a database administrator for a regional insurance company, working mostly from home now after years in an office, and he had always taken quiet pride in being the person who could find the error no one else could see. Divorced for many years and living alone, he had been managing the routines of older age with the same methodical discipline until a life-threatening illness shattered his sense that carefulness could keep him safe. What stayed with him most was not a single dramatic image but the bodily immediacy of that period: the rush of fear when his breathing changed, the sense that something inside him had turned without warning, and the hospital environment that became fused in his mind with mortal danger. When he thinks about that time now, he does not describe it as remembering in any ordinary sense. He says it can feel as if he is dropped straight back into it, as though the illness is happening again in the present tense. At those moments he can smell the sharp hospital odors again, the sterile chemical scent and the stale dryness of recirculated air, and the memory has a vividness that feels more solid to him than what he ate that morning or what he did the day before.

In the months after he survived the illness, Richard expected gratitude or relief to arrive and settle things. Instead, he found himself living as if the emergency had never ended. Even inside his own house, where he used to feel most at ease, he remained on guard. He checked the rooms without quite admitting to himself that he was checking them, paused to listen to his breathing, noticed every shift in temperature, every flutter in his chest, every sensation that might mean his body was failing again. He was troubled by how quickly fear could overtake him, but the fear was accompanied by anger and a quieter shame that he could not simply “get over” something that doctors told him was over. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous in a way he had not understood before, not only because illness could strike without warning, but because ordinary life now seemed to sit on top of catastrophe like thin ice.

Richard’s workday gave these reactions repeated opportunities to intrude. Sitting at his home workstation, monitoring overnight data jobs and responding to emails from younger colleagues, he could suddenly be pulled into the sensory immediacy of the illness by something as small as the smell of disinfectant after wiping down his desk, or the plastic-medical smell that lingered when he opened a cabinet where supplies from that period were still stored. For a moment the room no longer felt like his study; it felt as if danger had returned in full. He would go still, scanning his body and his surroundings, certain that he had to stay watchful. Even when no new symptom emerged, his body’s readiness itself frightened him. He had come to think of his body as an enemy of sorts, something that kept reacting as if he were still under threat, something he could not fully trust even when test results were normal and he was sitting safely at home in front of familiar screens.

Over time, this stance of vigilance narrowed his life. He was less willing to relax into evenings, less likely to let himself drift into absorbed concentration, because being unguarded felt reckless. He kept his phone close, moved through the house with an ear tuned to any sign that something was wrong, and experienced his own home as a place where he must remain prepared rather than a refuge. The emotional shift was just as stark. Richard said he had lost faith broadly and painfully: not only in the fairness of life, but in the idea that safety could be earned or that there was any dependable order beneath events. He spoke less of belief in a higher power than of a more general collapse of trust. Life, to him, now seemed arbitrary and hostile. That outlook had made him more distant with others. Though still competent at work, he kept interactions clipped and practical, less interested in the casual reassurances people offered because they sounded to him like things said by people who had not yet learned how quickly everything could change.

By the time he sought help, what troubled him most was the sense of being unable to leave the illness in the past. He was tired of memories that arrived with such force they felt more real than the present, tired of being ambushed by smell, tired of feeling watchful in his own living room. He did not come in describing a wish to become carefree; that seemed impossible to him, maybe even foolish. What he hoped for, more modestly and more urgently, was to stop living as though survival had never actually happened. What frightened him most was that this constant readiness meant he would spend whatever years remained to him braced against danger, unable to believe in safety even for an hour.
